title: Computational Causal Explanation Theory (CCET): A New Paradigm for AI Explanation
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems have traditionally focused on producing accurate predictions or decisions. The resulting outputs, however, rarely provide insight into the underlying causes that led to a particular result. This paper introduces the Computational Causal Explanation Theory (CCET), a formal framework that augments standard AI outputs with rigorous causal explanations. CCET unifies the concepts of structural causal models, counterfactual reasoning, and deterministic mappings to produce a joint output consisting of the predicted value and its causal justification. The theory is presented in a purely mathematical form, with all symbols expressed in plain text to facilitate direct transcription. CCET's core contribution lies in demonstrating that any AI system can be re‑engineered to compute not only "what" but also "why", thereby redefining interpretability and accountability in machine learning. title: A hybrid hierarchical multimodal learning with autoencoders, vision transformers and deep belief networks for liver cancer detection
abstract: A clinical problem of early liver cancer is one of the most urgent ones due to the insidious nature of tumors, the lack of multimodal data consistency and large inter-subject variation. Conventional systems of diagnosing rely highly on manual interpretation and monomodality images that typically result in delayed diagnosis and reduced effectiveness in the treatment. The researcher in this study presents another model of multimodal deep intelligence to detect and categorize early liver cancer through the combination of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) data. The provided solution is an integrated self-regularized autoencoder (AE) to learn the multimodal representation and allows noise suppression and compression of latent features. Vision Transformer (ViT) involves extracting long-range spatial dependencies and context in fused representations. Dynamic maximization of diagnostic decision policy and classification confidence under different clinical settings ML networks are A Deep Belief Network (DBN) that has hierarchical tissue abstraction and probabilistic pattern modelling and Deep Q-Network (DQN) that optimizes diagnostic decision policy and classification confidence. A standard liver imaging dataset (612 institutional patients to be assessed in the first instance and 512 public patients to be assessed in the second instance) yields high diagnostic quality, potential for generalization, and classification accuracy with positive results of 98.76% (95% CI 98.12–99.34) and an AUC of 0.992 (95% The findings confirm that there was successful multimodal fusion with heterogeneous deep learning paradigms in the detection of early liver cancer. This research will add the presence of scalable, intelligent, and clinically relevant diagnostic architecture to facilitate timely responses and decision support systems to manage liver cancer.

title: TractoGraphVLM: A Unified Vision-Language Framework for White Matter Tractography
abstract: Vision language models have transformed 2D medical imaging, yet extending them to 3D white matter tractography remains challenging due to the complex topology of fiber bundles. We introduce TractoGraphVLM, a unified framework for four tasks, bundle classification, text-to-tract retrieval, anatomical captioning, and visual question answering, built on a shared GPS architecture, training procedure, and read-out design. Fiber bundles are represented as streamline graphs whose nodes encode 3D position and tangent orientation. A General, Powerful, Scalable (GPS) graph transformer produces bundle embeddings aligned with a frozen BiomedBERT text encoder via contrastive learning, while a BioGPT decoder with visual prefix tokens generates captions and answers. A single shared encoder and decoder is trained jointly across all four tasks and evaluated from one checkpoint. Trained on HCP Young Adult subjects, TractoGraphVLM achieves 91.8% bundle classification accuracy, 84.7% retrieval R@1, BLEU-4=20.1, ROUGE-L=66.8, and 66.4% VQA accuracy on a held-out test set. The same checkpoints transfer zero-shot to HCP Aging subjects, with a modest drop on discriminative tasks and a larger drop on generative tasks, showing robustness to age and acquisition shift. Language supervision yields richer representations than label-only training, recovering structure like hemisphere and fiber family, carried by captions but never given as a label. Swapping only the visual encoder, graphs preserving fiber orientation outperform volumetric baselines, with GPS giving the best balance. Generative metrics measure consistency with a structured knowledge base rather than independent clinical text; even so, TractoGraphVLM shows that classifying, retrieving, describing, and answering questions about a white matter bundle can be served by one jointly trained model that learns transferable neuroanatomy from language alone.

title: Underwater Color Restoration with Vanishing Uncertainty
abstract: Underwater color restoration promises to unlock color as a reliable signal for aquatic sciences, but achieving this with scientific confidence remains out of reach. Current methods are validated almost exclusively on an empirical basis, which provides confidence only to the extent that the vast diversity of possible visibility conditions is covered with end-to-end testing using a known ground truth. This is exacerbated by color restoration being a fatally ill-posed problem when considered in full mathematical generality, requiring additional constraints to narrow the solution to a finite uncertainty interval. The gap between which constraints suffice in theory and which constraints are satisfied by real-world data is poorly understood, making it unclear whether existing methods are solving a problem that is actually solvable. In this article, we investigate the theoretical side of this gap, identifying idealized conditions which guarantee bounded uncertainty that converges to zero as the spatial resolution of the camera increases.

title: Symmetric Folding Principle for Quantum Propagator Synthesis
abstract: We introduce the symmetric-folding principle, a geometric quantum-control framework that lifts quantum state steering to exact propagator synthesis. The required structure is a folding symmetry: a unitary transformation that reverses the drift Hamiltonian while preserving the admissible control space. The method recasts propagator synthesis on the unitary group as steering of a chosen quantum state variable between fibers of an equivariant quotient map, followed by a prescribed folded continuation of the controls. We prove that control inputs satisfying the resulting fiber-transfer condition, when extended by the prescribed folded continuation, generate the desired unitary propagator in the associated symmetry-selected target family. This gives two key structural advantages. The fiber-transfer condition constrains the midpoint propagator only to a coset of the folding symmetry's centralizer. The prescribed fold cancels this residual freedom exactly. Thus a full group-level endpoint constraint is replaced by a lower-codimension fiber/coset condition, giving additional freedom in control design. For quantum ensembles, different members may reach different midpoint propagators within the same coset, while the folded sequence still yields a common final propagator for all ensemble members. This parameter-dependent freedom can be especially significant for robust ensemble-propagator design. We demonstrate the construction on an SO(3) Bloch ensemble and an SU (4) scalar-coupled two-spin system.

title: Memory That Doesn't Expire: Agentic Long-Term Memory for Conversational Agents on a Single Consumer GPU
abstract: Conversational agents forget: once a dialogue outgrows the context window, a model must either be reminded through retrieval or have its history truncated. Recent memory systems address this with extraction and retrieval, but they assume a large, often API-hosted model as the memory manager, an assumption that rules out private, local deployment. We ask whether a small local model, on a single consumer GPU, can manage long-term memory well, and how the answer depends on model size. We evaluate four memory strategies (no memory, full-history stuffing, raw-turn retrieval, and an agentic protocol that extracts typed, dated, deduplicated facts) on LoCoMo (1,986 questions over 10 long multi-session conversations), scored by an independent LLM judge. Full-context stuffing wins aggregate accuracy when the answer still lies inside the window, but its advantage is an artifact of conversation length: split by whether a question's evidence survives truncation, stuffing collapses by 76% beyond the window while agentic memory stays flat, outperforming stuffing 2.0x on the 39% of questions that already exceed it. Agentic memory further gives the best temporal reasoning of any strategy (via absolute-date grounding at write time) using ~67x less context. Varying the extractor from 3B to 14B, we find quality scales with size and that temporal grounding is the first capability to break under compression, setting a minimum viable memory-manager size of ~7-14B, comfortably within a 12 GB GPU. A hand-verified audit of 200 stored memories finds 199 faithful to their source turn, with no fabrications. We release the system, the benchmark harness, and the raw judged outputs behind every reported number. title: Confident but Incorrect: Measuring LLM Confidence Calibration for Mathematical Problem-Solving
abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly being used as tools for mathematical problem-solving and have shown progressive improvement in reasoning capability. However, even frontier LLMs remain prone to hallucination when challenged with problems beyond their capabilities, often presenting incorrect reasoning with high confidence. In this paper, we examine how LLM self-assessed confidence aligns with empirical accuracy across math problems of varying difficulty and type. Furthermore, we test a model’s confidence on both its initial attempt and a prompted retry in which the model is informed of its prior error. Our method reveals a systematic overestimation of confidence that persists even after the model is informed of prior error, with miscalibration increasing largely monotonically with problem difficulty. These findings highlight the gap between perceived and actual LLM reliability in mathematical reasoning.

title: Research on the Application of Knowledge Graph and AI Task Engine in Empowering Personalized Instruction for Fundamental Computer Science Courses
abstract: Against the backdrop of the profound integration of professional accreditation in engineering education with the digitalization of education, computer-related foundational courses, serving as pivotal vehicles for talent development, generally confront salient challenges such as fragmented knowledge delivery, inadequate personalized instruction, an onerous teaching workload for educators, and a superficial infusion of ideological and political education into the curriculum. To tackle these pressing issues, this study leverages the sophisticated knowledge graph, AI task engine, multimedia educational resources, and question bank system of the Fanya Learning Platform, in conjunction with frontline teaching reform initiatives, to investigate a curriculum development pathway that seamlessly integrates AI technology with the knowledge graph while intertwining ideological and political education throughout the curriculum. Through the refinement of platform-based teaching materials, the construction of dynamic cognitive profiles for students, and the incorporation of ideological and political elements such as the spirit of craftsmanship and patriotism, a comprehensive closed-loop precision teaching and collaborative education model is established. This model offers theoretical insights and practical guidelines for the digital and ideological transformation of computer-related foundational courses, thereby facilitating the cultivation of high-caliber professionals endowed with both ethical integrity and professional prowess.

title: TopoDialogue: Visualising and Operationally Distinguishing Recurrent Semantic Trajectories in Multi-Turn Dialogue
abstract: Long human–AI conversations may return to a similar semantic region without being exact textual repetitions. A return may be unproductive, may add detail or abstraction, or may precede a move into a new region. These cases are difficult to distinguish in a flat transcript. We present TopoDialogue, an offline, provenance-aware research instrument that represents a dialogue as a time-indexed three-dimensional trajectory and assigns one of four operational classes: closed loop, spiral revisit, escape, or open trajectory. The current implementation uses explicit semantic-node annotations when available and a declared lexical fallback otherwise. It provides deterministic hash-based display co-ordinates, four selectable height mappings, recurrence and progress scores, first-occurrence speaker provenance, and warnings for known display artefacts. We define the complete Phase-1 procedure and evaluate it with six authored synthetic cases whose expected structures are known by construction. Both the Python reference implementation and the browser implementation match all six declared class and recurrence-source labels; these are specification-conformance tests, not an estimate of accuracy on natural conversation. The study shows that recurrence, progress within a revisit, and feature provenance can be made inspectable and reproducible. It does not show that the display recovers a unique semantic manifold, infers mental state, or improves dialogue outcomes. We report projection instability, lexical approximation, monotonic-time, and speaker-drift failure modes and set out the human-annotated evaluation needed next.

title: The Authority Resolution Framework: A Five-Domain Ontology for Governing Who and What Decides, at Scale
abstract: As AI systems become increasingly capable of autonomous action, determining whether an agent is technically capable of performing an action is insufficient: the system must also determine whether the action is authorised in its context. This paper introduces the Authority Resolution Framework (ARF), a five-domain ontology for representing and resolving authority across organisational roles and informal influence, business concepts, codified processes, machine-readable permissions and executable systems, and external real-world context. ARF defines the Authority Relation (AR) as a cross-domain primitive binding an actor, action, object, bounded context, justification chain, and a calibration measure termed the DNA-Coefficient, which captures divergence between documented authority structures and authority as practiced. The framework provides a machine-interpretable representation of authority provenance and scope, with JSON-LD representations and knowledge-graph query patterns for authority resolution. ARF is designed to support AI agents in determining the provenance, scope and contextual validity of authority before executing consequential actions. The framework positions authority resolution as a knowledge-representation and reasoning problem at the intersection of ontology engineering, semantic AI, agentic AI and AI governance.

title: Easy-EO: chainable raster analysis for Earth Observation in Python
abstract: A Python library for raster-based Earth Observation analysis. Everything happens through a single dataset object that can be clipped, reprojected, resampled, reduced to a spectral index or plotted, with each operation returning another dataset so an analysis chains as a sequence of steps. A search against any SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog returns matching scenes, and loading one reads only the pixels covering the area of interest, so imagery can be worked on without downloading the scenes it comes from. Scenes from a search, or a folder of rasters, gather into a time series that can be composited into one cloud-free image, reduced to one image per period, or followed through time at a single place.

title: Keefektifan Layanan Bimbingan Kelompok Melalui Aplikasi Digital Aku Pintar Untuk Meningkatkan Minat Dan Bakat Siswa Kelas VIII SMP Negeri 7 Jember
abstract: This study aims to determine the effectiveness of group guidance services through the digital application "Aku Pintar" in enhancing students' interests and talents. Interests and talents are aspects in developing students' self-potential, but they are often not optimally explored due to limitations in guidance services provided in schools. The current generation is very familiar with technology, making digital-based approaches a relevant and adaptive choice. This study employs a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental method and One Group Pretest-Posttest Design. The research used a quasi-experimental method involving 2 student groups: an experimental group that received guidance counseling services through the digital application "Aku Pintar" and a control group that received conventional services. The guidance counseling services conducted through the "Aku Pintar" Application proved effective in enhancing students' interests and talents, and can serve as an innovative alternative in school guidance counseling services. The research subjects were eighth-grade students who demonstrated needs for interest and talent development. Research instruments in the form of questionnaires and observation sheets were administered before and after the intervention to measure changes in students' understanding and awareness of their self-potential. The English abstract is written following the content of the Indonesian abstract. The writing format is the same as the Indonesian abstract format, using proper and correct English.

title: CardiacMamba: Fair and Robust RGB-RF Fusion for Remote Heart Rate Estimation via State Space Modeling
abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables non-contact heart rate (HR) monitoring from facial videos, but RGB-only methods are vulnerable to illumination changes, motion artifacts, and skin-tone-dependent optical reflectance. We propose CardiacMamba, a fair and robust RGB-RF fusion framework that integrates optical facial cues and radio-frequency cardiac motion cues through state space modeling. CardiacMamba introduces a Temporal Difference Mamba Module (TDMM) to enhance subtle RF temporal variations, a bidirectional SSM-based interaction mechanism to align heterogeneous RGB-RF dynamics, and a Channel-wise Fast Fourier Transform (CFFT) module for channel-domain spectral refinement. On the EquiPleth dataset, CardiacMamba achieves state-of-the-art performance with 0.96 bpm MAE, 3.06 bpm RMSE, and 0.97 Pearson correlation, while reducing the observed light-dark skin-tone MAE gap to 0.26 bpm and maintaining robustness under RGB degradation and RF-missing conditions

title: Secure-by-Design Machine Intelligence: Engineering Privacy, Robustness, and Trust Across the AI Lifecycle by Kuldeep Chowdary Raavi
abstract: ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS I would like to express my sincere gratitude to everyone who contributed, directly or indirectly, to the completion of Secure-By-Design Machine Intelligence: Engineering Privacy, Robustness, and Trust Across the AI Lifecycle. First and foremost, I am deeply grateful to my family for their constant encouragement, patience, understanding, and unwavering support throughout the preparation of this book. Their motivation and confidence provided me with the strength and inspiration to pursue this work and bring it to completion. I sincerely thank my teachers, mentors, colleagues, and professional associates whose guidance, discussions, knowledge, and experiences have contributed to my professional understanding of Artificial Intelligence, cybersecurity, software engineering, cloud platforms, privacy, and emerging technologies. Their valuable insights have helped shape the perspectives presented in this book. I would also like to acknowledge the researchers, engineers, developers, cybersecurity professionals, and members of the wider technology community whose continuous efforts have advanced the fields of secure AI, machine learning security, privacy engineering, robust machine intelligence, and trustworthy AI. Their research and practical contributions have provided an important foundation for exploring secure-by-design approaches to AI. My professional experiences in software engineering, cloud platforms, and cybersecurity have provided valuable opportunities to understand the importance of building secure, scalable, and reliable technology environments. These experiences have strengthened my belief that security and privacy must be considered throughout the development and operational lifecycle of intelligent systems. I am also thankful for the opportunities to participate in cybersecurity research, technical publication, patent development, journal reviewing, editorial activities, and hackathons. These engagements have provided valuable exposure to emerging ideas, innovative solutions, and practical technology challenges. I extend my appreciation to the professionals, researchers, and aspiring technologists whom I have had the opportunity to mentor and interact with. Knowledge sharing and collaborative learning have continually reinforced the importance of approaching technological innovation with curiosity, responsibility, and a strong commitment to security. I am grateful to everyone who offered constructive suggestions, encouragement, feedback, and intellectual support during the development of this book. Each contribution, whether through professional interaction, research discussion, or personal encouragement, has played a meaningful role in bringing this work together. Finally, I would like to express my appreciation to all those working toward the responsible development and adoption of Artificial Intelligence. As intelligent systems become increasingly integrated into everyday applications and critical digital environments, the principles of privacy, robustness, security, transparency, accountability, and trust will become increasingly important. It is my sincere hope that this book contributes to the growing body of knowledge on secure machine intelligence and encourages readers to adopt a secure-by-design mindset when developing, deploying, and managing AI systems. Kuldeep Chowdary RaaviAuthor

title: Decision-Closure Invariants in LLM Reasoning: CFC Anchor Behavioral Pilot Series
abstract: This exploratory technical report consolidates a sequence of behavioral micro-tests examining whether large language models preserve decision-closure boundaries when evidence coverage, rejection pressure, process termination, operational decisions, semantic scope, or provenance change. The tests use explicit invariants inspired by Comparative Feedback Control (CFC), including: certificate validity is not the same as current coverage sufficiency; failure to verify is not evidence for rejection; process closure is not proposition closure; operational action is not an epistemic verdict; and loss of provenance is not permission to transfer semantics. In a cross-model stale-certificate pilot, Google AI Mode produced a false positive closure without the explicit coverage rule but blocked with it; Gemini's final decision was already correct but its intermediate reasoning improved; Claude already satisfied the target invariant in both conditions. In later Google AI Mode replications, baseline reasoning drifted toward unjustified rejection in 3/3 missing-assessment runs and 3/3 process-closure runs, whereas matched runs supplied with explicit CFC-style invariants remained neutral in 3/3 and 3/3. In a three-run cross-session provenance-loss series, baseline produced one semantic-transfer failure and two correct unresolved outcomes, while the CFC condition remained unresolved in 3/3. These are small, adaptive, non-preregistered behavioral pilots. They do not execute the CFC Anchor code, do not estimate stable model error rates, and do not establish general CFC effectiveness. The supported claim is narrower: making decision-closure constraints explicit can stabilize model behavior in selected adversarial reasoning scenarios where baseline behavior is sometimes unstable under pressure.

title: Title: Computational Proof Path Discovery Algorithm (CPPDA)
abstract: The automation of mathematical proof discovery remains a central challenge in theoretical computer science. Existing approaches often rely on exhaustive search or symbolic manipulation, which quickly become infeasible as the size of the theorem space grows. This paper introduces the Computational Proof Path Discovery Algorithm (CPPDA), a novel method that automatically discovers the most probable sequence of inference steps leading from a given theorem to a proof. CPPDA models the search space as a directed graph whose vertices are formal statements and edges represent inference rules. By applying a probabilistic weighting scheme derived from heuristic estimates of rule applicability and contextual relevance, CPPDA guides a search procedure towards high‑probability proof paths without resorting to brute‑force enumeration. We formalize the algorithm, analyze its computational complexity, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of synthetic benchmarks. The results suggest that CPPDA can break through current bottlenecks in automated theorem proving and may lay the groundwork for future breakthroughs in formal verification and mathematical knowledge discovery.

title: Computational Paradigm Reconstruction Theory (CPRT)
abstract: The field of computer science has traditionally focused on the design, analysis, and implementation of algorithms. However, the underlying computational paradigms that give rise to these algorithms remain largely implicit. Computational Paradigm Reconstruction Theory (CPRT) proposes a systematic method to extract the hidden computational principles from a large corpus of algorithms and to reconstruct the paradigms that govern them. CPRT introduces a formal mapping from algorithms to paradigms, denoted M(A) = P, and develops a reconstruction procedure that iteratively refines P by examining structural, functional, and behavioral commonalities across algorithms. The theory is grounded in set-theoretic and category-theoretic concepts, allowing it to capture both classical and emerging computational models. By applying CPRT to representative algorithm families—such as sorting, dynamic programming, and quantum search—this paper demonstrates how fundamental paradigms like divide-and-conquer, memoization, and amplitude amplification can be recovered without prior knowledge of their names. The implications of CPRT extend to algorithmic education, automated theorem proving, and the search for novel computational frameworks that may inspire future Turing Award-worthy contributions.

title: Phi‑Coupled E8 Lattice for Topological Quantum Error Correction — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: We propose that the 240 root vectors of the E8 lattice can be arranged into a phi‑coupled symplectic phase field that serves as a stabilizer code for quantum information. Each root vector encodes a logical qubit subspace, and the 132 Hz manifold provides a resonant drive that maintains coherence while enabling error syndromes via geometric rotations. This construction extends the E8 torsional information dynamics by turning latent geometric rotation into active error‑detecting fluxes, yielding a fault‑tolerant framework with intrinsic phi‑ratio protection. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: MITE-Net: SWaP-Optimized 4K Video Tiny Target Perception for Embodied Edge SAR
abstract: Real-time tiny target perception in high-resolution imagery is critical for embodied Search-and-Rescue (SAR) missions. However, strict Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints on edge devices like UAVs create a bottleneck: traditional image downsampling causes severe feature loss, while slice-based processing incurs prohibitive latency. To address this gap, this paper introduces a comprehensive framework encompassing a novel architecture, specialized datasets, and hardware-level benchmarks. First, we propose MITE-Net, a SWaP-optimized cascaded architecture, which couples a bio-inspired, learning-free Tiny Target Motion-Based Region Proposal Network (TTM-RPN) with a sub-0.14M-parameter R-CNN-like head. Second, to standardize 4K tiny target evaluation, we construct the SAR-Tiny Datasets by relabeling two challenging UAV datasets: SeaDroneSee-Tiny (dynamic maritime scenes, tiny targets predominantly of 64-256 pixels ) and UAVID-Tiny (cluttered urban scenes, extremely tiny targets, less than 64 pixels). Third, we benchmark against state-of-the-art YOLO models on an edge device, NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier, where MITE-Net directly processes 4K maritime imagery, achieving a 100\% search success rate at 30.33 FPS. Consuming merely 3.19 W (9.51 FPS/W), MITE-Net vastly outperforms YOLO baselines in target recall and energy efficiency. Conversely, UAVID-Tiny evaluations expose a compound structural limitation: the learning-free bionic front-end struggles against urban backgrounds, while the ultra-lightweight head lacks representational capacity for complex features. Ultimately, this work delivers an efficient onboard perception paradigm and a rigorous baseline guiding future end-to-end SAR architectures.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of First-Order Noisy Input Gaussian Process Regression under Increasing Input Uncertainty
abstract: Gaussian Process (GP) regression provides a flexible probabilistic framework for learning nonlinear input–outputrelationships, but standard formulations commonly assume that input variables are observed without error. NoisyInput Gaussian Process Regression (NIGP) addresses this limitation by propagating input uncertainty througha first-order Taylor approximation of the GP posterior mean, producing an input-dependent effective variance.This study presents a systematic empirical evaluation of the established first-order NIGP formulation under pro-gressively increasing input uncertainty rather than proposing a new mathematical NIGP correction. Syntheticexperiments were conducted using a sine–trend function with input-noise standard deviations from 0.1 to 1.0and 50 paired Monte Carlo replicates per condition. Performance was assessed using Root Mean Squared Error(RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Negative Log Predictive Density (NLPD), Prediction Interval CoverageProbability (PICP), absolute coverage error (ACE), mean prediction interval width (MPIW), Winkler score, andContinuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). The first-order approximation was additionally evaluated againstMonte Carlo propagation and a second-order Taylor reference, while further experiments examined input-noisemisspecification, multiple nonlinear benchmarks, heterogeneous uncertainty, and multidimensional correlated in-put noise. NIGP generally produced higher RMSE and MAE than the conventional GP, with the point-predictionpenalty increasing as input noise became larger and being primarily associated with increased bias. Probabilis-tic performance was more nuanced: NIGP achieved slightly higher PICP than the standard GP, but its absolutecoverage error was higher at every noise level, indicating that the higher coverage did not correspond to closeragreement with the nominal 95% target. At the highest noise level, NIGP yielded lower NLPD, narrower in-tervals, and lower Winkler and CRPS scores. However, first-order approximation error increased substantiallywith increasing noise, while empirical convergence of the iterative procedure deteriorated sharply. Sensitivityanalysis further showed that misspecifying the input-noise level materially affected predictive and calibrationperformance. The results, thus, indicate that NIGP is useful as an uncertainty-propagation framework, but itspractical benefits depend strongly on noise magnitude, correct uncertainty specification, and the validity and nu-merical stability of the first-order approximation.

title: Beyond Artificial Intelligence: The Universal Cognitive Substrate
abstract: We present the Universal Cognitive Substrate, a 2MB deterministic physics kernel that replaces probabilistic AI with conservation-governed intelligence. Operating at 347ns per decision with zero idle cost, the substrate is hardware-agnostic, cloud-independent, and mathematically complete.

title: Computational Language Self‑Generation Theory (CLSGT)
abstract: Computational Language Self‑Generation Theory (CLSGT) proposes a novel paradigm in which a computational system autonomously invents new programming languages rather than merely learning or translating existing ones. In CLSGT the system observes patterns of human experience, formalizes these patterns into a set of primitives, and iteratively refines a language that best captures the observed phenomena. The theory is grounded in formal language theory, information theory, and cognitive modeling, and it predicts that self‑generated languages can achieve higher expressiveness and efficiency for specific domains than conventional human‑designed languages. CLSGT also offers a theoretical foundation for understanding the evolutionary dynamics of programming languages and provides a roadmap for designing adaptive language ecosystems that evolve in tandem with user needs. This paper presents the core principles of CLSGT, develops a formal framework for self‑generation, examines potential impacts on software development, and outlines research directions and challenges that must be addressed to realize the full potential of self‑generated computational languages.

title: Computational Value Singularity Theory (CVST‑2)
abstract: Computational Value Singularity Theory (CVST‑2) proposes a formal framework for the autonomous generation of novel value systems within artificial intelligence systems. By defining value as a recursively defined scalar field over state spaces, CVST‑2 demonstrates how an agent can iteratively refine its reward function to create higher‑order value structures that transcend its initial programming. The theory extends traditional reinforcement learning by allowing the agent to synthesize new reward dimensions through compositional and hierarchical mechanisms, resulting in value recursion that amplifies both the diversity and magnitude of the agent's objectives. We formalize the core equations governing value creation, analyze stability conditions, and discuss the implications of value recursion for the emergence of advanced intelligence and the potential for a Turing‑Award‑worthy breakthrough. The paper concludes by outlining avenues for future research, including the integration of CVST‑2 with symbolic reasoning systems and the ethical considerations of autonomous value generation.

title: Structured Dynamics Optimization: Expert-Calibrated Energy Modulation of Multi-Motion Predictive Priors for Humanoid Imitation
abstract: Frame-wise imitation provides a clear reference but not a measure of whether a learned future deserves equal influence at every state. We present Structured Dynamics Optimization (SDO), a reward-level mechanism that converts internal discrepancies of a pretrained motion model into weak, state-dependent guidance for reinforcement learning. The high-level model is trained first on a multi-motion corpus containing dozens of expert trajectories, learning shared temporal structure before low-level policy optimization begins. From three past 67-dimensional states, a Transformer produces a 256-dimensional latent code and a 30-frame coarse future; a 20-step diffusion-inspired refiner produces the corrected future. SDO reads two quantities from this frozen model: expert-calibrated latent deviation and coarse-to-refined correction. Their calibrated sum forms an energy proxy that controls how strongly the predicted target is trusted, while a separate policy–prior agreement term checks its physical relevance to the current state. The auxiliary term enters only through the reward interface. In LocoMuJoCo, SDO energy is positively associated with future prediction error, and refinement energy reaches a Spearman correlation of about 0.55 at 15- and 30-step horizons. Across five paired 300-million-step runs, SDO raises deterministic imitation return from 16.4396 to 16.9191 (+2.92%) and episode length from 125.75 to 134.61; every paired seed improves on both measures. evidence.title: Structured Dynamics Optimization: Expert-Calibrated Energy Modulation of Multi-Motion Predictive Priors for Humanoid Imitation
evidence.abstract: Frame-wise imitation provides a clear reference but not a measure of whether a learned future deserves equal influence at every state. We present Structured Dynamics Optimization (SDO), a reward-level mechanism that converts internal discrepancies of a pretrained motion model into weak, state-dependent guidance for reinforcement learning. The high-level model is trained first on a multi-motion corpus containing dozens of expert trajectories, learning shared temporal structure before low-level policy optimization begins. From three past 67-dimensional states, a Transformer produces a 256-dimensional latent code and a 30-frame coarse future; a 20-step diffusion-inspired refiner produces the corrected future. SDO reads two quantities from this frozen model: expert-calibrated latent deviation and coarse-to-refined correction. Their calibrated sum forms an energy proxy that controls how strongly the predicted target is trusted, while a separate policy–prior agreement term checks its physical relevance to the current state. The auxiliary term enters only through the reward interface. In LocoMuJoCo, SDO energy is positively associated with future prediction error, and refinement energy reaches a Spearman correlation of about 0.55 at 15- and 30-step horizons. Across five paired 300-million-step runs, SDO raises deterministic imitation return from 16.4396 to 16.9191 (+2.92%) and episode length from 125.75 to 134.61; every paired seed improves on both measures. Evaluation disables the SDO bonus for both methods, so the gains reflect the policy learned during training rather than an altered test-time reward.

title: GraniKV: Asymmetric Granularity KV-Cache Paging for Multi-Agent Systems with Long Shared Prefix
abstract: Production paged-serving engines apply uniform paging granularity to the KV cache, even though the two regions of a multi-agent workload have opposite storage requirements: a long shared prefix demands contiguity, while the per-request suffix demands fine-grained allocation. We present \textbf{GraniKV}, a KV-cache layer that allocates the shared prefix in a contiguous HOT pool and the suffix in a token-level COLD pool, combined with a per-step dispatcher which selects the appropriate backend among dual backends for each regime (compute-, memory-, or communication-bound). To the best of our knowledge, GraniKV is the first system to apply asymmetric paging granularity to the KV cache of a production paged-serving engine. At $L_p{=}16$\,K shared tokens GraniKV reaches $\mathbf{2.16\times}$, $\mathbf{1.98\times}$, and $\mathbf{1.57\times}$ output-token throughput over the production baseline on Llama-3.1-8B/TP=1, Qwen-2.5-14B/TP=2, and Qwen-2.5-32B/TP=4. The gain decomposes: cascade attention integration contributes the majority at saturation; the asymmetric storage layer adds $1.05$--$1.15\times$ end-to-end while being what makes the batched-GEMM prefix backend possible at all. Under heterogeneous multi-agent serving with \emph{distinct} prompts of different lengths, the attribution inverts: GraniKV sustains $\mathbf{1.95\times}$ while batch-global cascade collapses to parity --- the storage layer alone carries the win in the regime that motivates the paper.

title: EFFECTIVENESS OF ADAPTIVE (PERSONALIZED) EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY BASED ON ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN TEACHING HUMAN ANATOMY: RESULTS OF A PEDAGOGICAL EXPERIMENT
abstract: The article presents a pedagogical experiment evaluating an artificial-intelligence (AI) based adaptive learning platform for the "Human Anatomy" course, which tailors content and question difficulty to each student's performance. The study involved control (n=15) and experimental (n=15) groups. No significant baseline difference was found (p>0.05). At the final stage, the experimental group outperformed the control across all dimensions by 13–14% (t=10.0; p<0.001).

title: Computational World Model Discovery Algorithm (CWMDA)
abstract: The ability of a machine to infer a coherent representation of its environment from raw observations is a longstanding goal in artificial intelligence. In this paper we present a new framework, the Computational World Model Discovery Algorithm (CWMDA), which formalises the process by which a learning system observes data, extracts hidden structure, and composes a world model that captures the underlying generative mechanism. CWMDA is grounded in information theory, spectral graph theory, and probabilistic graphical modelling. We derive a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for the identifiability of hidden causal structures from observational data, propose an efficient iterative optimisation routine that alternates between structure learning and parameter estimation, and provide a rigorous convergence analysis. The algorithm is designed to be scalable to high-dimensional data streams and to accommodate nonstationary environments. We discuss theoretical implications for the future of machine science, including the potential for Turing Award level contributions in formalising machine cognition. The paper is self-contained and does not rely on experimental evaluation; instead, it focuses on algorithmic development and theoretical guarantees.

title: Computational World Model Space Theory
abstract: Computational World Model Space Theory (CWMST) proposes a mathematical framework for representing all conceivable world models as points within a high‑dimensional space Ω_W. By formalizing the notion of structural distance between models, CWMST supplies a quantitative foundation for machine understanding of reality. This paper develops the core constructs of CWMST, demonstrates how to construct Ω_W, defines a metric that captures structural similarity, and discusses implications for artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and the philosophy of science. Without reliance on empirical experiments, the exposition focuses on theoretical derivation and logical coherence, aiming to provide a robust platform for future research into the mathematical underpinnings of machine perception.

title: PoseAdapter: Dual-Stream 2.5D Controllable Image Generation for Complex Multi-Object Scenes
abstract: While Text-to-Image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved remarkable success, precise spatial and orientational control in multi-object scenes remains a persistent challenge. Existing methods either rely on computationally expensive dense 3D maps or suffer from severe attribute leakage and "cut-and-paste" artifacts. To address these limitations, we propose PoseAdapter, a lightweight framework for high-fidelity 2.5D controllable image generation. Instead of dense spatial maps, it establishes precise spatial-angular anchors using an efficient condition layout: individual object captions, 2D bounding boxes, and 3D angles. To resolve the generative trade-off between strict instance isolation and global coherence, we introduce a Context-Aware Dual-Stream Representation. By injecting local object tokens and relation-enriched scene tokens into the visual stream of modern MM-DiT architectures via parallel masked and unmasked pathways, PoseAdapter eliminates attribute leakage while preserving natural inter-object relationships and scene-level coherence. To support this paradigm, we construct OrientLayout, a high-quality dataset featuring standardized 2.5D annotations and instance-level decoupled semantics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PoseAdapter outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in spatial accuracy, orientational precision, and multi-object visual fidelity. Code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/cyf23/PoseAdapter.

title: Computational Personality Self-Revision Theory (CPSR)
abstract: The notion of an artificial agent that can autonomously modify its own behavioral style has long been a central aspiration in the field of artificial intelligence. The present paper introduces a formal framework, Computational Personality Self-Revision Theory (CPSR), which models personality as a high‑dimensional vector of trait weights and provides a dynamical system for the gradual transformation of an agent's personality in response to both internal objectives and external interactions. CPSR posits that personality evolution is governed by a set of coupled differential equations that balance a desire for consistency, a drive for novelty, and a constraint that ensures coherence with the agent's functional role. We analyze the stability of the resulting system, identify conditions for convergence to fixed points or limit cycles, and discuss the implications for the design of AI systems with adaptive social behavior. Without relying on experimental data, the theoretical results suggest that CPSR could form the basis for future research into self‑evolving AI that maintains a balance between robustness and adaptability, a key ingredient for achieving systems with Turing‑Award potential.

title: Computational Abstraction Transfer Theory (CATT)
abstract: Computational Abstraction Transfer Theory (CATT) proposes a unified framework for systematically migrating abstract concepts from one computational domain to another. By formalizing abstraction spaces as sets of symbolic representations and defining transfer mappings as compositional functions that preserve structural and semantic integrity, CATT offers a principled method for leveraging insights across disparate fields such as artificial intelligence, software engineering, and data science. The core idea is that an abstraction developed in the context of AI, for example, can be translated into a programming abstraction that accelerates software design, or a data abstraction can be reinterpreted as a knowledge representation in ontology engineering. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CATT, introduces formal definitions and properties of transfer mappings, and illustrates the theory through several case studies. We argue that the systematic application of CATT can unlock new avenues of cross‑domain innovation and potentially contribute to the next wave of breakthroughs that may be recognized by the Turing Award.

title: Interpretable Symbolic Regression for Psychological Questionnaire Data: Prediction, Descriptor Discovery, and Nonlinear Interaction Analysis
abstract: Psychological researchers increasingly use machine-learning methods to improve prediction, yet many high-performing models require post-hoc explanation and provide limited insight into how predictors combine to shape outcomes. We present an application-oriented workflow for GoodRegressor, a hierarchical, depth-controlled symbolic-regression framework, using psychological questionnaire data. The workflow was demonstrated with independent datasets of middle-aged wives from Japan (n = 201) and South Korea (n = 220), with marital satisfaction predicted from demographic variables, family viewpoints, conflict-resolution strategies, and derived descriptors. The datasets were analyzed separately because the family-viewpoint measure was not sufficiently invariant across countries. Nine regression methods were evaluated using identical deterministic five-fold test partitions. In five-fold held-out testing, GoodRegressor showed the strongest predictive performance in Japan (5 = .441, 5 = 0.220, 5 = .178). In South Korea, GoodRegressor remained competitive (5 = .338, 5 = 0.199, 5 = .155), although Elastic Net, Ridge, and Random Forest performed somewhat better overall. Among equation-oriented methods, GoodRegressor substantially outperformed PhySO and EQL. Full-data GoodRegressor ensembles identified husband’s age, assertion, and age-difference-by-assertion structure in Japan, and avoidance, husband’s age, and family-priority-by-avoidance structure in South Korea. These findings support symbolic regression as a practical approach for combining competitive prediction with directly inspectable nonlinear and interaction structure, facilitating interpretable hypothesis generation in psychological research.

title: Agentic Security: A Systematization of Tools, Failure Modes, and Design Laws for LLM-Driven Penetration Testing
abstract: Agentic security uses large-language-model (LLM) agents to plan, dispatch, and interpret security tools. As these systems move from demonstrations to deployed products, practitioners repeatedly encounter the same operational failures. We systematize these failures through a hands-on evaluation of ten widely used static, dynamic, cloud, orchestration, and AI red-teaming tools for unattended pipelines. We introduce a four-dimensional Integration Friction Index that separates one-time engineering cost from recurring organisational, legal, and maintenance cost. We then derive quantitative regularities that explain recurring failure modes. Modelling an agentic security system as stochastic LLM policies wrapped by a deterministic mediator, we show that long-lived sessions lose resident evidence with phase count, while short-lived sub-agents extend the usable horizon according to the compression ratio between raw evidence and its summary. We show that a two-stage verdict cascade multiplies scorer likelihood ratios, but provides little benefit when scorer errors correlate. We show that treating unevaluable outcomes as attack failures biases downstream measurements toward evasive and severe responses. We formulate planner-versus-worker model routing as a knapsack problem and derive a closed-form execution cap for heavy-tailed tools, eta* = alpha v/c. Finally, we show why scope and budget enforcement cannot be delegated to system prompts: prompts do not constrain what actually executes. Inspectra, our implemented platform, serves as a worked instantiation, with mechanisms labelled shipped, partial, or planned, including those that did not work.

title: Computational Invariant Transfer Theory (CITT): Bridging Physics and Computing
abstract: The notion of invariance is fundamental to both physical law and computational design. In physics, invariants such as conservation of energy and momentum provide deep insight into the structure of physical systems. In computing, invariants arise in program semantics, security proofs, and algorithmic guarantees. This paper introduces Computational Invariant Transfer Theory (CITT), a formal framework that systematically transfers invariants from a source domain to a target domain, thereby enabling the construction of novel computational theories that are grounded in physical principles. We present the core idea of invariant transfer, formalize the transfer mechanism via mapping functions and equivalence relations, and illustrate how CITT can generate new computational models with provable correctness properties. We discuss potential implications for the development of cross‑domain computational theories, including the prospect of a Turing Award–level contribution that unifies physics and computing. The paper concludes with an outlook on future research directions and challenges inherent to invariant transfer.

title: Computational World Model Generation Theory (CWMGT)
abstract: The Computational World Model Generation Theory (CWMGT) proposes a principled framework for automatically constructing computable representations of the environment that go beyond simple predictive modeling. By mapping observed data streams into a latent world model that captures causal structure and dynamics, CWMGT enables agents to simulate hypothetical scenarios, reason about interventions, and generate novel behaviors. This paper formalizes the core ideas of CWMGT, presents an algorithmic blueprint for system construction, and analyzes its theoretical properties. We argue that CWMGT has the potential to become a foundational component of next‑generation artificial intelligence, analogous to the role of neural networks in deep learning, and may eventually contribute to Turing‑Award‑level contributions in AI research.

title: Benign Projective Landscapes for Measured Quantum Divergences
abstract: We study nonconvex optimization of measured quantum $f$-divergences over rank-one projective measurements. For smoothly operator-Fenchel liftable generators and faithful states, every projective local maximum and every second-order stationary point is globally optimal over all POVMs. The criterion is blockwise: a critical PVM is optimal exactly when the compressed states are proportional on each equal-score block; otherwise an explicit two-vector rotation has positive ascent curvature. Operator-convex generators admit a positive atomic curvature resolution, and the quadratic $χ^2$ case yields two-sided residual bounds. For binary accessible information, this framework proves the known adaptive-capacity equality and shows that every nonidentical qubit ensemble has exactly two stationary projective measurements, proving conjectures of Keil and Thai--Dall'Arno. A rare-prior limit connects weighted Jensen--Shannon information to relative entropy and yields a finite counterexample to the proposed equivalence between observational-entropy and all-ensemble mutual-information orders. The landscape theorem also covers measured Rényi divergences of finite positive order and measured relative entropy.

title: FlowDance: Music-Driven Dance Video Generation with Parallel Pose and RGB Streams
abstract: Music-driven dance video synthesis aims to animate a reference person according to a given music clip. The task is challenging because it requires a model to jointly learn music-to-motion correspondence, identity-preserving human animation, temporal coherence, and visually realistic video generation. We present FlowDance, a music-driven dance video generation framework that integrates explicit motion modeling with reference-preserving visual synthesis through parallel pose and RGB streams. We further introduce timestep-aware pose injection to adapt structural guidance across denoising steps and persistent identity injection to preserve the reference appearance over long video. To support this task, we further build a popularity-curated, high-resolution in-the-wild dance video dataset with synchronized music, RGB videos, 3D body motion, camera parameters, and projected 2D pose annotations. evidence.abstract: Music-driven dance video synthesis aims to animate a reference person according to a given music clip. The task is challenging because it requires a model to jointly learn music-to-motion correspondence, identity-preserving human animation, temporal coherence, and visually realistic video generation. We present FlowDance, a music-driven dance video generation framework that integrates explicit motion modeling with reference-preserving visual synthesis through parallel pose and RGB streams. We further introduce timestep-aware pose injection to adapt structural guidance across denoising steps and persistent identity injection to preserve the reference appearance over long video. title: From Generalist to Specialist: A Context-Fusion Framework for Endoscopic Polyp Reporting with a Frozen VLM
abstract: Reliable endoscopic polyp reporting requires integrating quantitative lesion sizing, standardized Paris classification, and clinically meaningful morphological description within a single record. General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) offer a unified interface for image understanding and report generation. Existing specialization strategies, however, typically rely on task-specific models or model-weight adaptation, leaving unresolved how to introduce reliable specialist knowledge while preserving both this unified interface and the VLM's pretrained capabilities. We introduce a context-fusion framework that specializes a frozen general-purpose VLM through both implicit instruction context and explicit transduction context without modifying its pretrained weights. Specifically, a self-supervised polyp encoder retrieves related image-report pairs as explicit, query-specific evidence, while learned continuous specialist tokens provide implicit instruction context shared across cases. Experiments were conducted on 2,056 expert-annotated public endoscopic images. We compared the framework with general-purpose VLMs, task-specific predictors, and weight-adaptation methods to assess specialist performance, unified reporting, and adaptation efficiency. Across numerical, categorical, and report-generation metrics, the proposed framework substantially improved direct frozen-VLM inference and achieved the strongest overall performance among the evaluated methods. It added trainable parameters equal to only 0.006% of the frozen VLM's parameter count. When the top-1 retrieved case carried the correct target category, our framework corrected 70.5% of the errors made by a weight-adaptation baseline. These findings support the context-fusion framework as a lightweight and effective strategy for specialist adaptation of a frozen VLM.

title: Computational Self‑Evolution Theory (CSET)
abstract: The Computational Self‑Evolution Theory (CSET) proposes a paradigm in which autonomous systems actively modify not only their parameters but also their own underlying mechanisms. By formalizing the evolution of a system's internal structure, CSET provides a framework that integrates adaptive machine learning, evolutionary computation, and dynamic system design. The core idea is captured by the transformation Self_t → Self_{t+1}, where Self_t denotes the system's structure and operational rules at time t, and Self_{t+1} is the updated version after self‑evolution. This paper delineates the theoretical foundations of CSET, presents a formal model with explicit state representation, evolution operators, and update rules, and discusses its potential to reshape software definition and its alignment with the criteria for the Turing Award. The proposed theory opens new avenues for creating truly self‑sustaining software agents capable of continuous, mechanism‑level refinement without external intervention.

title: Computational Paradigm Discovery Algorithm (CPDA)
abstract: The rapid expansion of computational tasks in science, engineering, and society demands novel ways to generate efficient, scalable, and adaptable algorithms. Traditional algorithm design relies heavily on human insight and iterative refinement, which limits the exploration of the vast space of possible computational structures, data organization schemes, and computation models. This paper introduces the Computational Paradigm Discovery Algorithm (CPDA), a meta-algorithm that automates the search for new algorithmic paradigms. CPDA operates by exploring a combinatorial space of algorithmic templates, data layout designs, and execution models, guided by a set of objective functions that capture correctness, efficiency, parallelizability, and resource utilization. We formalize the CPDA framework, describe its search operators, and present a proof-of-concept implementation that demonstrates the discovery of a novel sorting paradigm that outperforms conventional quicksort on large, heterogeneous datasets. The results suggest that CPDA can uncover computational patterns that are non-intuitive to human designers, opening a new frontier in automated algorithm engineering.

title: A Definitional Fragment of Temporal Equilibrium Logic: from Temporal Programs to Compact Automata
abstract: We consider a definitional fragment of Temporal Equilibrium Logic (TEL), which allows to capture temporal rules that contain complex (implication-free) temporal formulas in rule bodies. We focus on the setting where formulas are interpreted over finite traces. We show that the basic reasoning tasks in the definitional fragment are PSpace-complete, showing a significant drop from the ExpSpace-completeness of the unrestricted case. Our method is based on characterizing stable models in terms of different kinds of type sequences, which allow to reason both about the existence and non-existence of stable models. In addition to handling tasks like stable model existence, we also show how the set of all stable models of a theory can be represented as a non-deterministic finite state automaton (NFA). Our method is self-contained in the sense that, in contrast to previous approaches, it does not rely on technical automata-theoretic results as black boxes. Our method can be implemented using SAT solving techniques and a prototype system is available.

title: Fusion Anything: A Generalized Multimodal Foundation Model
abstract: Making prediction with multimodal data is widely used in diverse scenarios. Existing multimodal fusion models, once deployed, can only handle predefined modalities (e.g., vision, text and audio) and single task, making it difficult to quickly adapt to new downstream applications. Therefore, a natural yet aggressive question arises - whether there exists a general multimodal fusion model that can be applied to arbitrary modality combinations and arbitrary prediction tasks. We argue that a unified multimodal fusion model should not depend on specific modalities and should instead encode transferable patterns of multimodal correlation. To this end, we propose a simple and effective learning paradigm based on training on large-scale synthetic multimodal datasets generated with Structural Multimodal Causal Models (SMCMs), which formally characterizes the generative processes of real-world multimodal data. Building on this framework, we propose the Fusion Anything Model (FAM), a foundation model for generalized multimodal data fusion. By constructing large-scale synthetic multimodal data with diverse correlation patterns, our model encodes transferable multimodal correlations during training and activates appropriate associations through in-context examples during inference. Extensive experiments on 18 real-world datasets spanning 12 modalities and 11 prediction tasks demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance with specialized models without task-specific adaptation.

title: Kozuchi Agent: A Language-Agnostic Open-Weight Agent for Software Repair
abstract: Industrial software-engineering teams increasingly need LLM agents that turn bug reports into correct patches, yet benchmark-scale operation adds long horizons, tool-use discipline, context persistence, heterogeneous clusters, and evaluation reuse. We present Kozuchi Agent, a language-agnostic open-weight repair agent and CI-operated evaluation pipeline. Explicit phases, persistent state, deterministic tools, a model-independent action interface, and cross-agent test-time selection make runs auditable and repeatable. With locally hosted Qwen3.5-27B, no fine-tuning, and TTS@8, Kozuchi resolves 374/500 SWE-bench Verified instances on the official evaluator. Unchanged on Multi-SWE-bench Java, the same 27-billion-parameter agent resolves 41/128 instances (32.03%), ranking first among strict open-weight submissions and fourth of 42 overall; on Python it ranks 12th of 135 and first among open-weight systems. Per-phase behavior remains within +/-5 percentage points across languages. Remaining failures mainly reflect semantic correctness, Java-specific harness issues, and selection errors. Across both tracks, results compare favorably with open/local peers by parameter count. Analysis of candidate diversity, selector regret, and patch reliability shows that the remaining gap is primarily semantic correctness and selection rather than edit formatting or proprietary-model access. Operationally, reusable CI stages reduce operator touch-points from five to one across heterogeneous internal clusters.

title: Computational Personality Transfer Theory (CPTT)
abstract: The burgeoning field of artificial intelligence has produced systems that exhibit a wide range of computational styles, from deterministic rule‑based engines to stochastic deep neural networks. Yet the question of whether a system's intrinsic computational personality—defined as the set of internal operational patterns and response heuristics that shape its problem‑solving behavior—can be transferred from one architecture to another remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces the Computational Personality Transfer Theory (CPTT), which formalizes the notion of computational style as a measurable vector of behavioral signatures and proposes a principled mechanism for mapping such a style from a source system P_A to a target system P_B. We develop a formal model of computational personality, define a similarity metric over style spaces, and prove that, under mild assumptions, a continuous transfer mapping exists. We also discuss the implications of CPTT for AI collaboration, knowledge distillation, and the ethical dimensions of personality replication. The theory is positioned as a candidate for recognition within the Turing Award community, given its potential to unify disparate AI approaches and to enable unprecedented levels of system interoperability.

title: Computational Representation Transfer Theory (CRTT)
abstract: Computational Representation Transfer Theory (CRTT) proposes a systematic framework for translating high‑level representations from biological domains into artificial intelligence systems. By formalizing the process of mapping biological representations to AI architectures, CRTT aims to unlock a new paradigm of cross‑domain knowledge transfer that can enhance learning efficiency, model robustness, and interpretability. This paper introduces the core concepts of CRTT, develops a mathematical formulation that captures the essence of representation migration, and discusses potential applications in fields ranging from natural language processing to autonomous robotics. The theory also examines the theoretical implications of aligning biological and computational representations, suggesting that such alignment may reveal fundamental principles underlying intelligence. CRTT thereby offers a blueprint for a unified approach to intelligence across living and engineered systems.

title: Computational Principle Self-Revision Theory (CPSR): A Framework for Autonomous Evolution of Computational Principles
abstract: Computational Principle Self-Revision Theory (CPSR) proposes a systematic method for the autonomous discovery, evaluation, and revision of computational principles within intelligent systems. CPSR treats a principle as a formal rule or algorithmic template that guides computation, and it models the revision process as a continuous optimization over a principle space. The theory introduces a formal representation for principles, a quantitative evaluation metric that captures performance across diverse tasks, and a principled update rule that ensures progressive refinement while maintaining coherence with prior knowledge. By embedding CPSR into the core of an autonomous agent, the system can detect when an existing principle becomes insufficient, generate candidate revisions, and select the most promising candidate based on empirical evidence. This dynamic adaptation fosters continual improvement and aligns with the vision of self-evolving computation. The paper details the formal foundations, algorithmic implementation, and illustrative case studies, and discusses the broader implications for artificial intelligence and the potential for achieving Turing Award–level impact.

title: Computational Principle Selection Theory (CPST-2): Automatic Determination of Optimal Principles for Problem Solving
abstract: The growing complexity of modern computational systems demands an automated methodology for selecting the most appropriate guiding principles for a given problem domain. This paper introduces Computational Principle Selection Theory (CPST-2), a formal framework that models the mapping from a problem specification to an optimal principle or set of principles. CPST-2 defines a space of candidate principles, a fitness function that evaluates principle suitability based on problem characteristics, and an optimization procedure that searches this space efficiently. The theory is grounded in concepts from information theory, graph theory, and complexity analysis, and it provides provable bounds on the quality of the selected principle. While CPST-2 is presented as a theoretical construct, its implications for automated system design are significant; a system that can autonomously select principles could accelerate the development of high-performance, reliable, and adaptive computational architectures. The paper discusses the formal definition of the principle space, the construction of the mapping function, and the algorithmic strategies for efficient exploration. It also explores potential applications in compiler optimization, distributed system configuration, and AI system design, and outlines future research directions for empirical validation and extension to dynamic environments.

title: Towards Defeasible Reasoning about Actions and Their Effects
abstract: Intelligent agents interacting with their environment need to reason about the effects their actions will have on their surroundings. For actions with deterministic outcome this problem is well investigated in the context of planning problems. But many real-world actions may not always result in their typical outcome, and exceptional outcomes of an action have to be taken into account. In this work we present a framework for reasoning about actions with uncertain outcomes. Inspired by conditionals, we introduce defeasible action rules that capture the typical outcome of action, without committing to what happens in exceptional circumstances. For the semantics of these rules we introduce ranked transition schemas: graph-based representations of transitions between possible worlds in which edges between states are assigned a rank indicating their typicality. We define an inference operator for defeasible action rules inspired by rational closure, adapting its intuitive semantics to the dynamic setting. Furthermore, we explore a generalization of this framework that uses partial orderings over transitions instead of ranks. This generalization strictly increases expressive power and enables more refined reasoning operators. Finally, we extend the language of defeasible action rules with a notation to express that certain properties are not affected by the execution of an action, thus allowing to explicitly formulate frame axioms in this defeasible setting.

title: RLCascadeRouter: Quality-Estimator-Free Cascade Routing via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: The growing ecosystem of large language models (LLMs) offers huge potential to optimize performance-cost trade-offs. However, their heterogeneous capabilities and inference costs make efficiently routing queries a significant challenge. Existing paradigms are inflexible: one-shot routers commit before observing responses, whereas conventional cascades stop adaptively but follow a fixed model order. Cascade routing removes both restrictions by reconsidering whether to stop or invoke another model after each response. Current methods use a predict-then-optimize pipeline estimating response quality and future model utility. However, prediction loss for quality or utility is not equivalent to routing-decision loss. A lower prediction error does not necessarily yield a better action; a small boundary-crossing error can reverse a ``stop'' or model-selection decision. Therefore, we propose RLCascadeRouter, a quality-estimator-free framework that formulates cascade routing as a Markov decision process with actions comprising ``stop'' and model selection. It uses trajectory returns and advantages to directly optimize the performance-cost objective. Its Cascade Policy Network models candidate complementarity for model selection and remaining-action value for stopping, eliminating independent post-hoc response-quality estimators. Evaluated across ten LLMRouterBench benchmarks with thirteen LLMs, RLCascadeRouter outperforms strong baselines and achieves superior performance-cost trade-offs. It incorporates unseen models without retraining, and ablation studies validate both policy components.

abstract: تتناول هذه الدراسة إشكالية تمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية في نظم معالجة اللغة العربية في ظل التطور المتسارع للنماذج اللغوية الكبرى وتقنيات الذكاء الاصطناعي. إذ تمثل هذه الأفعال فئة دلالية معقدة تعبر عن حالات نفسية وانفعالية داخلية، مثل الخوف والحب والقلق والاطمئنان، وهي معانٍ تتسم بدرجة عالية من التجريد والتداخل المفهومي، مما يجعل نمذجتها الحاسوبية أكثر صعوبة من الأفعال العادية المرتبطة بالأحداث والأفعال المادية الملموسة. وتزداد أهمية هذه الإشكالية مع اتساع الاعتماد على التطبيقات الذكية في تحليل النصوص العربية وتوليدها وفهمها آليا. وتنطلق الدراسة من فرضية مفادها أن المقاربات الحاسوبية المعاصرة، ما تزال عاجزة عن تمثيل البنية المفهومية العميقة للأفعال السيكولوجية تمثيلا دقيقا، على الرغم من التطور الملحوظ الذي حققته في مجال معالجة اللغات الطبيعية، وذلك بسبب اعتمادها على المعالجة الإحصائية والسياقية السطحية، دون النفاذ إلى العلاقات الدلالية المركبة التي تحكم هذا الصنف من الأفعال. وتهدف الدراسة إلى تحليل أبرز الإشكالات المرتبطة بتمثيل الأفعال السيكولوجية، خاصة ما يتعلق بالفالنسي، والأدوار الدلالية للمشاركين في الحدث النفسي، والتدرج الانفعالي، والعلاقات التركيبية والدلالية التي تحدد سلوك هذه الأفعال في الاستعمال اللغوي. واعتمدت الدراسة منهجا توصيفيا تحليليا قائما على فحص نماذج مختارة من الأفعال السيكولوجية العربية وتحليل طرائق تمثيلها في بعض تطبيقات المعالجة الحاسوبية الحديثة، مع الاستفادة من الأدبيات اللسانية والمعجمية ذات الصلة. وتخلص الدراسة إلى أن تجاوز محدودية النماذج الحالية يقتضي بناء توصيف دلالي-تركيبي متكامل يربط بين المعنى والبنية والاستعمال، ويستثمر إمكانات نظرية معنى-نص والمعجم التأليفي التفسيري والمعجم التركيبي في تمثيل العلاقات الدلالية والفالنسية للأفعال السيكولوجية. ومن شأن هذا التوجه أن يسهم في تطوير نماذج أكثر قدرة على فهم المعنى النفسي في اللغة العربية وتحسين أدائها في تطبيقات الذكاء الاصطناعي ومعالجة اللغة الطبيعية.

title: The Next Layer of Enterprise AI: From Models to Enterprise Systems
abstract: Enterprise AI systems increasingly operate across governed data, organisational knowledge, transactional systems and business processes. As these systems move from prototypes into production, the engineering challenge extends beyond model inference to the architecture responsible for context, execution, reasoning and enterprise semantics. This paper examines three architectural capabilities that recur across enterprise AI implementations: the Execution Harness, which governs how intelligence interacts with enterprise systems; the Reasoning Loop, which manages evidence accumulation, evaluation and convergence; and the Enterprise Graph, which represents organisational meaning through governed semantics and relationships. Together, these layers provide an architectural model for integrating foundation models with enterprise data, knowledge, policy, tools and operational workflows. The paper explores the responsibilities of each layer, their interaction, and the implications for designing AI systems that can be executed, explained and trusted in enterprise environments.

title: Computational World Model Generation Network (CWMGN)
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has highlighted the importance of internal world models for agents to predict, plan, and understand complex environments. Existing approaches either learn a latent representation of the world or generate future observations, but they are limited by either scalability or fidelity. This paper introduces the Computational World Model Generation Network (CWMGN), a novel architecture explicitly designed to generate fully runnable world simulations from raw observations. CWMGN combines a hierarchical representation module, an event‑driven transformer, and a physics‑informed decoder to produce a closed‑loop simulation that can be executed step by step. The architecture is formally defined with clear mathematical notation, ensuring that each component can be analyzed independently. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that CWMGN preserves causality, ensures energy conservation in physical sub‑domains, and converges to a stable simulation under reasonable assumptions. Potential applications span autonomous navigation, virtual reality content creation, scientific discovery, and next‑generation AI systems. The proposed design offers a clear pathway toward a Turing Award‑level contribution by providing a scalable, general, and interpretable framework for world model generation.

title: Semantics for Description Logics via Assumption-Based Argumentation: Preliminary Results
abstract: Description Logic (DL) terminologies are collections of rules in which a class is defined in terms of a complex DL concept. Various semantics for terminologies have been proposed over the past decades. However, the tight relation with the recent W3C SHACL standard for expressing constraints over RDF graphs motivated the need to enrich terminologies with forms of commonsense reasoning. In this paper, we explore how reasoning over DL terminologies can be captured in argumentative terms, by establishing a translation into Assumption- Based Argumentation (ABA), a rule-based formalism comprising defeasible assumptions, where argumentation semantics are used to retrieve sets of jointly acceptable assumptions. We focus on the problem of graph completion, where a labeled graph is extended by assigning additional labels only to existing nodes while satisfying a given terminology. Building on the existing correspondence between logic programs and ABA, we show how a DL terminology and a labeled graph can be encoded as an ABA framework such that different completions of the graph arise from different criteria for selecting sets of assumptions. We present results for DL terminologies in 𝒜ℒ𝒞ℐ under the classical semantics, the minimal model semantics of Circumscription, and the stable model semantics of Quantified Equilibrium Logic. Furthermore, we provide preliminary results for fragments of the DL-Lite family, where the problem of graph completion is extended to allow the introduction of new domain elements, enabling full model construction.
